summary: Defines version 2 of the Internet Stream Protocol, a limited-use experimental protocol for carrying real-time streams such as voice and video with reserved resources. It revises the earlier version in IEN-119 based on experiments, and it was replaced by RFC 1819.

plainLanguage.summary: Regular mail is delivered whenever. This is more like reserving a lane on a road so a live voice call can get through smoothly.

subtitle: An experimental IP-layer protocol for real-time data streams with reserved network resources.

tldr.problem: IP was not designed to guarantee delivery rates or bounded delays, making it unsuitable for real-time applications like voice and video that have predictable bandwidth and latency requirements.
tldr.mechanism: ST-II introduces streams: directed trees from an origin to target destinations with reserved bandwidth and delay parameters. Each stream is set up in advance with resource reservations, and data packets are forwarded efficiently using Hop Identifiers (HIDs) rather than looking up full stream names.
tldr.outcome: ST-II provided proof-of-concept that real-time multimedia communication over packet networks was feasible with advance setup and resource reservation. It was replaced by RFC 1819 and is now historic, but its concepts influenced later QoS work including the Reservation Protocol (RSVP).

facts.label: Core innovation
facts.value: Advance setup with resource reservation for deterministic delay

today: RFC 1190 is now Experimental and was superseded by RFC 1819. ST-II was never deployed at scale in the Internet, but it pioneered important concepts for real-time communication: the idea of reserving network resources before sending data, specifying bandwidth and delay requirements, and detecting/recovering from failures. These concepts influenced the design of RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol) and remain relevant in Quality-of-Service (QoS) and network slicing today.

sections.title: Real-Time Communication and Resource Reservation
sections.content:
IP was designed to deliver packets with best-effort service, making no guarantees about delay, delivery order, or whether packets arrive at all. Real-time applications like voice (Network Voice Protocol) and video (Packet Video Protocol) need predictable, bounded delays and dedicated bandwidth to function well.

ST-II (Stream Protocol Version 2) solves this by introducing the concept of streams: end-to-end paths with pre-allocated resources. Before sending data, an application requests its local ST agent to create a stream to one or more destination hosts. The stream setup process reserves bandwidth and buffer space along the path, and once established, data packets can be forwarded with minimal delay and high reliability.

A FlowSpec describes the bandwidth, delay, and reliability characteristics of data a stream will carry. It includes desired maximum bandwidth and delay, minimum acceptable values, packet size, transmission rate, and a duty factor for variable-rate traffic like voice (which has silent periods). During stream setup, agents at each hop attempt to reserve the resources described in the FlowSpec.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular internet is like a highway where anyone can drive anytime and traffic jams happen. ST-II is like reserving a clear lane just for your call so you get a smooth ride. You tell the network what you need before you start.

sections.title: Stream Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
An ST Agent is any device running ST-II: a host agent originates or receives data, while an intermediate agent is a router forwarding ST packets between networks. A stream is a directed tree carrying data from one origin host to one or more target hosts.

Each stream is identified by a globally unique Name. For efficient forwarding, each hop in the tree is marked with a Hop Identifier (HID) negotiated between adjacent agents. A hop is an edge connecting a previous-hop agent (toward the origin) to one or more next-hop agents (toward targets). When network-layer multicast is available, multiple edges to next-hops can be served by a single multicast group with a common HID.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the origin as a TV station, targets as viewers, and hops as the cables and relay towers carrying the signal. Each connection gets a shorthand label (HID) so forwarders know where to send each packet without looking up the whole stream name.

sections.title: Stream Setup and Management
sections.content:
To create a stream, the origin sends a CONNECT control message to each next-hop agent, containing the target list, FlowSpec, and other parameters. Each intermediate agent on receiving a CONNECT message must: negotiate a HID with its previous-hop, map the targets to next-hops using a routing function, reserve local resources, and propagate CONNECT messages to its next-hops with partitioned target lists.

When targets receive the CONNECT message, they inquire with the application whether to accept the stream. Each accepting target sends an ACCEPT message back toward the origin. An established stream can be modified without disruption: the origin can add new targets, remove specific targets, or change the FlowSpec using a CHANGE message. To tear down a stream, the origin sends a DISCONNECT message. A stream can optionally be monitored for failures; if a network link or agent fails, agents can detect it and attempt automatic recovery using a pruned depth-first search to bypass the failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The origin calls out: 'I want to send to B, C, and D; will you help?' Each hop asks the next ones, 'Can you reach your targets?' When all say yes, the stream is ready. You can later add friends, remove them, change quality, or hang up.

sections.title: Control Messages and Data Forwarding
sections.content:
The ST Control Message Protocol (SCMP) handles all stream management. SCMP is a request-response protocol using retransmission with timeout to ensure reliability. Control messages use Virtual Link Identifiers (VLIds) to quickly dispatch messages to the correct stream's state machine at each agent.

Once a stream is established, data transfer is simple and efficient. The origin sends ST data packets with a short ST header containing the HID, protocol number, and payload. Intermediate agents forward data packets using the HID for fast lookup of the forwarding list. Network-layer multicast is used where possible to replicate the packet to multiple next-hops. This separation of expensive setup from cheap data forwarding allows ST to support real-time streams with low overhead and predictable latency. ST-II also includes options like PTP (Point-to-Point) for single-target streams and FDx (Full Duplex) for bidirectional communication with reduced overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: SCMP is how agents talk to set up and manage the stream—it's the phone call before the video starts. Once the call is connected, data packets are tiny and fast because the routing is already figured out.
